title: Awe and kindness
hookLine: after gazing up at tall trees, people helped more in a study (Piff et al.)

cards: A handful of pens hits the ground. The person who dropped them says oops and bends to gather them. You're standing right there.
Do you crouch down and help, and how many do you pick up? It's a tiny moment, the kind nobody remembers by lunchtime, which is exactly why a team of psychologists used it.
They wanted to know whether something that came just before, something that had nothing to do with pens, could change how many a stranger would pick up. What came before was a minute of looking up.

teach.b: The study was led by Paul Piff, with colleagues including Dacher Keltner. First, the setup. Some people stood in a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees and looked up into them for a short while.
Others stood in the same spot but looked up at a tall building nearby. Same place, same task; only the view was different. Second, the pens.
Afterward, a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens, apparently by accident.
The people who had gazed up at the trees picked up more of them. A small kindness, but measured. The tree group also reported feeling less entitled, less like the world owed them.

Third, the researchers' explanation: the small self, the same idea from the awe walk selfies. Awe shrinks a person's sense of their own importance, not in a crushing way, but in a way that makes room.

In their account, under very tall trees a person's own concerns shrink back to size, and other people come back into view. Their other studies pointed the same way: awe nudged people toward generosity.
Fourth, trees and wonder have kept company a long time.

teach.h: THE TREES OF THE WOOD REJOICE.
teach.b: In the Psalms, in the King James words: "then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice."
The poet pictures the trees themselves caught up in praise. The scientists never mentioned rejoicing trees; they counted pens. Two ways of standing among trees, and both begin by looking up.

how: Some people make a habit of stopping under tall trees or in front of big views and looking up for a while, and then turning their attention to someone nearby who could use help.

o: a naturalist who measured the world's tallest eucalyptus trees
the researcher who found tall buildings make people feel powerful
the researcher whose tall-tree study found awe made people help more

games.q: you've just spent a short while looking up into very tall trees. a stranger drops a handful of pens. what did the study find people like you tended to do?
o: pick up more of the pens.
games.why: the people who gazed up at the trees picked up more pens than those who looked at a tall building.

practice: Stand under a tall tree if there's one near you, or find the tallest thing you can see from a window, or bring back the tallest tree you remember.
Let your head tip back and follow the trunk up, branch by branch, to where it meets the sky, feeling your own size against it. Then bring to mind one person nearby who could use a small hand.

wordCard.voice: Paul Piff. The researcher whose study found that people who gazed up at tall trees helped a stranger more, in what he called the small self. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: tall trees. Under them, your own concerns shrink to size, and other people come back into view. I'll be here tomorrow.
